lede: Two things happen one after the other, and the second depends on how the first went. A tree diagram lays every possible pair of outcomes out on its own branch, with a probability on each, so a question that sounded tangled becomes a list you can add up.
can: Draw a two- or three-stage tree, with and without replacement
Multiply along a branch and add the branches that qualify
Use the complement to answer 'at least one' in a single line

text: One branch for every way it can go

md:
A pencil case holds 11 pens: 7 blue and 4 black. Two are taken out one after the other, and the first is not put back.
Each draw has two outcomes, so there are four ways the pair can come out. A tree gives each of them a branch and writes the probability along it.

md: A first branch is the colour's share of what is there. A bag of 4 green and 3 yellow marbles gives $\dfrac{4}{7}$ for green and $\dfrac{3}{7}$ for yellow, and the pair adds to 1: $\dfrac{4}{7} + \dfrac{3}{7} = 1$.

prompt: On the pen tree, what is written on the very first branch, for the first pen being blue?
explain: 7 of the 11 pens are blue, and nothing has been taken yet, so the denominator is still 11.

text: 1. Without replacement changes the second stage

md: If the first pen is not put back, the case holds one pen fewer for the second draw, so every second-stage denominator drops by one. A numerator drops only on a branch where a pen of that colour has already gone.

title: Why the second stage depends on the first
md: A second-stage branch carries a probability **given** what happened above it. After a blue pen, one fewer blue is left; after a black pen, all 7 blue are still there. The first draw changed what is left.
With the marbles: take a green one out and keep it. $7 - 1 = 6$ marbles are left, $4 - 1 = 3$ of them green, so the next green branch carries $\dfrac{3}{6}$.

prompt: On the pen tree, the first pen taken is blue. How many pens are left in the case for the second draw?
explain: 11 - 1 = 10. The pen is not replaced, so every second-stage denominator on the tree is 10.

md:
Two rules do all the work.
**Along a branch, multiply.** $P(\text{blue then blue}) = \dfrac{7}{11} \times \dfrac{6}{10}$
$= \dfrac{42}{110}$, which cancels to $\dfrac{21}{55}$.
**Across branches, add.** Branches are separate ways for the same event to happen, and they cannot both occur, so their probabilities add.

prompt: Using the pen tree, what is $P(\text{both pens are black})$? Give a fraction or a decimal.
explain: $\dfrac{4}{11} \times \dfrac{3}{10}$ is $\dfrac{6}{55}$: multiply along the branch, with the denominator dropping to 10.

text: 3. Events on more than one branch

md:
'Both the same colour' happens on two branches, blue-blue and black-black. Work each one out, then add.
$P(\text{same}) = \dfrac{21}{55} + \dfrac{6}{55}$, which is $\dfrac{27}{55}$.
Multiplying those two instead of adding is the slip the reports name: multiplying asks for both branches to happen at once, which is impossible.

title: What the reports keep finding
md: Candidates work out each branch correctly and then multiply the two results instead of adding them. The same reports also ask for exact fractions: switching to decimals part-way through has cost accuracy marks.

prompt: Two branches of the pen tree each give 'the pair is the same colour'. What do you do with their two probabilities?
options: Add them, because the two branches cannot both happen
Multiply them, because both are needed
Take the larger of the two
answer: Add them, because the two branches cannot both happen
explain: The pair is either blue-blue or black-black, never both. Separate branches add: $\dfrac{21}{55} + \dfrac{6}{55}$ is $\dfrac{27}{55}$.

md:
A pair with one pen of each colour can come out blue then black, or black then blue. Both branches count, so both products go into the answer: blue then black, $\dfrac{7}{11} \times \dfrac{4}{10}$, plus black then blue, $\dfrac{4}{11} \times \dfrac{7}{10}$.
Counting one order only halves the answer, and that is exactly what examiners report.

title: Tree Diagrams
why: Building a tree and reading pairs off it, with and without replacement. The three-stage tree and the conditional read are the steps this unit adds on top.

prompt: On the pen tree, blue-then-black has probability $\dfrac{14}{55}$ and black-then-blue has the same. What is $P(\text{one of each colour})$?
explain: The two orders add: $\dfrac{14}{55} + \dfrac{14}{55}$ is $\dfrac{28}{55}$. One order alone would give half of that.

md:
Adding every branch that has at least one black pen means three branches. Taking the one branch that has none away from 1 means one line.
$P(\text{at least one black}) = 1 - P(\text{both blue})$, which is $1 - \dfrac{21}{55} = \dfrac{34}{55}$.
Examiners have said outright that subtracting from 1 is the simpler route, and that adding every branch invites an arithmetic slip.

prompt: On the bus tree, $P(\text{on time both mornings}) = 0.7225$. What is $P(\text{late on at least one of the two mornings})$?
explain: $1 - 0.7225 = 0.2775$. 'At least one' is everything except the branch with none.

md:
A third pen adds a third stage, and the denominators fall again to 9. There are eight paths now, but nothing new to learn.
All three blue is $\dfrac{7}{11} \times \dfrac{6}{10} \times \dfrac{5}{9}$, which gives $\dfrac{210}{990}$ and cancels to $\dfrac{7}{33}$.
With replacement every stage would keep the denominator 11, and the answer would be different.

prompt: On the three-stage pen tree, the first two pens taken are blue. What is the probability that the third is blue as well?
explain: Two blue pens have gone, so 5 blue are left among 9: $\dfrac{5}{9}$.

md: Every probability on these trees is an exact fraction, and it is worth keeping it that way to the last line. Turning one into a rounded decimal early and then adding rounded decimals is a reported cause of lost accuracy marks.

Multiply numerators and denominators, then cancel at the end: $\dfrac{4}{11} \times \dfrac{3}{10} = \dfrac{12}{110}$, which cancels to $\dfrac{6}{55}$. Convert only if the question asks for a decimal.

explain: $\dfrac{5}{8} \times \dfrac{4}{7}$ is $\dfrac{5}{14}$. Keeping 8 on the second denominator would have given 0.31.

md: **Kept, or put back?** In Summer 2024 some worked with replacement throughout when the items were kept. Put back, two blue pens are $\dfrac{7}{11} \times \dfrac{7}{11} = \dfrac{49}{121}$; kept, they are $\dfrac{7}{11} \times \dfrac{6}{10} = \dfrac{21}{55}$. Read which one the question says before drawing a branch.

**'Not all the same' by subtraction.** The same paper asked for different colours, where adding every qualifying branch meant six products. Take the two same-colour paths from 1 instead: for three pens, $1 - \dfrac{7}{33} - \dfrac{4}{165} = \dfrac{42}{55}$.

prompt: A bag holds 3 red and 2 blue beads. A bead is taken, put back, and a second bead is taken. What is $P(\text{both red})$? Give a fraction or a decimal.
explain: Put back, the bag is the same for both draws: $\dfrac{3}{5} \times \dfrac{3}{5}$ is $\dfrac{9}{25}$. Kept, the second draw would have been $\dfrac{2}{4}$.
